units.title: Can't see the ground (part 2)
units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: The first thread hit the reply limit, so here's part two. For anyone new: I run a tower crane on night lifts in Halvard, sixty metres up, and after about one in the morning the site floods go off and all I can see below me is the hook light swinging. I asked who else works somewhere they lose sight of the floor at night. Carry on, it's been the best company I've had all month.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: Care home, ground floor, so I can always see the ground in theory. But the garden lights are on a timer and they go off at one, and after that the big window by the night desk only shows me the corridor reflected back. I keep thinking someone is walking behind me and it is my own cardigan on the chair. Sorry, this is long. I like this thread.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Container port. Stacks five high. From the gatehouse I see aisles, not ground. Camera 7 looks straight down aisle K and past the second lamp it is black to the fence. 03:00 round done, gates checked, reefers humming. Patrolled, nil found.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Sleep lab tech. My room has no window at all, which I recommend. The interesting bit about losing the ground: the brain dislikes a visual field with no anchor and starts inventing movement. A single light in the dark will appear to drift even when it is perfectly still. It's called the autokinetic effect. Crane, keep one fixed reference in view, the edge of the cab frame, anything solid, and the hook light should stop wandering.

units.author: lh_crane_halvard
units.text: Dmitra, that's exactly it. The hook light walks about when I stare at it, and I've been half convinced the jib was swinging. I put a strip of yellow tape across the bottom of the cab window as a sort of horizon last week without knowing why it helped. Now I know it has a name. Learn something every night up here.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Ninth floor, respiratory. Our windows look down on the staff car park, which is lit by the orange lamps that make everything look like an old photograph of itself. So I can see the ground, I just don't quite believe it. Tea's gone cold again. Back to it.

units.author: lh_wren_nights
units.text: Not mine. I keep picturing a different one. A camper, with the desk pushed up under the window so you sit with your back to the room. Past the glass it's trees, close together, more than anyone could count. The ground goes dark before the trees do. You'd sit there and watch the gap between them.

units.author: lh_wren_nights
units.text: I mostly watch the screen, not the window. Data entry, columns of numbers, a desk fan for the noise. There's a blackout blind behind me and I honestly couldn't tell you what's outside it. A car park, probably. Probably fine.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text:
wren that's either a poem or the saddest job advert I ever read, which is it
anyway mine is a cab and I can see the ground fine it's the potholes I can't see, the council paints round them now instead of filling them

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text:
blackout blind is the only way, I sleep days with one of those and a rolled towel along the bottom of the door
my neighbour thinks I'm a vampire anyway, the fan for noise works too, mine sounds like a small plane

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Wren, honest question, is this a bit? It's fine if it's writing, half this forum is writing. Just flag it as fiction so nobody reads it as a real place. I spend my nights watching stories get taller with every caller and I'd rather this thread didn't.

units.author: skeptic_orla
units.text: Radio producer. The overnight studio is in the basement of the Sound FM building in Port Ammet: no windows, one clock, one red light. If the red light's off I'm alone with the playout system. When I come up the stairs at six the pavement is the first ground I've seen all night, and it is usually covered in gulls' opinions.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Porter at Port Ammet General. We have the tunnel between the old block and the new one: four hundred metres of lino, no windows, and one strip light by the stores end that maintenance swear blind is fine. You can't see the ground because you're under it. After a while the trolley wheels tell you where you are, every join in the floor has its own clunk.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Not a night worker, only a poor sleeper above a bookshop in Tollinby. From my window I see the square, the memorial and the one lamp the council forgot to put on the new timer. Some nights a cat crosses under it and I feel I have been handed a very short story. Tonight it was a fox, which is a longer one.

units.title: The van that doesn't run its engine
units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Some of you remember my idling van, which turned out to be a driver having a kip with the heater on. I gave him a roll and we're friends now. Tonight there's a different one, white, parked exactly where the streetlight stops by the fish market steps. Engine off, no lights. I've had two batches in and out and it hasn't moved. Not sure why I'm telling you. It's just there.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Baker, I have form with vans at the edge of lights, as people here know. My advice after four nights of mine: note the plate if you can read it, note the time, and don't walk over on your own. Control's advice to me was 'it's a van'. Both pieces of advice can be true at once.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: With the engine off in this cold, whoever's in it is either very well wrapped or not in it. Most likely a market trader who parks early to get a good spot and walks home or sleeps in the cab with a bag. In Halvard the fish lot is full by four. Not exciting, but most things at four in the morning aren't.

units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Dmitra you might be right, the traders do start about five. It's only early for them. I've written the plate on a scrap of greaseproof and tucked it under the till. Meanwhile the sourdough is proving beautifully, if anyone needs a cheerful note: big blisters, smells like a cellar in the best way.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Coriveth too. Market steps are on my drive home at six. If it's still there I'll slow down and look. Not getting out, just looking from the car, and I'll post what I see.

units.author: lh_baker_coriveth
units.text: Thank you, that's kind. Still there. One thing keeps bothering me: anyone sitting in a cab in this frost would fog the windscreen, and it isn't fogged at all, it's clear and white at the edges. Back to the ovens now. The croissants don't care what's parked outside.

units.title: Caller described her porch light and hung up
units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Utilities helpline, overnight. A woman calls about a flickering porch light, which is a fair thing to ring a power company about, except halfway through she stops talking about the bulb and starts describing exactly where the light ends on her lawn. 'It reaches the birdbath and then it doesn't.' Then she said thank you and hung up. Logged it as a lighting query. I am not reading into it. Typing between calls, more in a sec.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Second half, sorry: the script says offer an engineer visit for any flicker, and I never got the chance. Her number came up as a landline in the coastal district, so probably an older lady with a dodgy fitting and nobody to chat to. Meanwhile our hold music this week is a pan-pipe version of a song I can't name and it is ending me slowly.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: People do that, I think. My nan used to ring the electricity board to tell them the street was dark. It wasn't a complaint, it was company. Biscuit the beagle says hello, by the way; he's on day four of a boarding stay and has eaten a sock, which we retrieved, which I won't describe.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Kennel, that's a nicer reading and I'm taking it home with me. Tell Biscuit socks are not a food group. Seventeen calls since, every one of them about a bill, two about a bill they've already paid. Normal service resumed.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: Reading this between centrifuge runs. 'It reaches the birdbath and then it doesn't' is going to live in my head all week. Not in a scary way, in a sentence-I-wish-I'd-written way. Back to pipetting, eleven samples to go.

units.title: Frost on the gallery rail
units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: A clear night on the western coast, the first in a while. The gallery rail had furred with frost by midnight and I could write my initials in it. From up there the beam goes out and comes round, and under it the sea is flat as slate, and then it is dark again until the beam returns. I have been counting the seconds between, the way I did as a boy. Twelve. Always twelve.

units.author: lh_kennel_orrin
units.text: Your posts are the best thing on here. Clear and cold on the flats too. The dogs love a frost, they come back in with it on their whiskers. Pepper the collie tried to eat a frozen puddle tonight and gave it nought out of ten.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: Same coast, different town, no gallery, just a staff car park with one lamp and the windscreens frosted in rows. Your twelve seconds is going on a sticky note by my headset for the next angry caller. Count to twelve, then speak.

units.title: Mid-week check-in: what's on your desk tonight?
units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: Post-chapter me reporting in. On my desk: a cold dumpling, my supervisor's comments printed out because I refuse to read them on a screen, a stress ball shaped like a brain, and a sticky note that says 'breathe'. The lab is empty except for the freezer alarm, which is practising. What's on yours?

units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: Counter. A scratch-card display, a jar of pens nobody returns, and a pair of reading glasses a man left four days ago. I've put them in lost property, which is a crisp tub. He'll be back. They always come back for glasses.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: The night book, a flask, the handover sheet, and a little glass vase Mrs Aird's daughter brought in after the funeral. The staff keep it on the desk now. We put a sprig from the garden in it most nights. It's frost tonight, so it's rosemary, and the whole desk smells of Sunday dinner.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Ward desk: obs charts, a box of chocolates from a family that says 'to the night angels', which is lovely, and next year's holiday rota with my name on Christmas for the fourth year running, which is less lovely. The orange creams are already gone. Back to it.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text:
dashboard, two phone mounts because the first one snapped, a tin of mints for the ones who've had a few, and a parking ticket I am appealing on principle
anyway desk is a strong word for it

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: No desk, I'm a picker, but on the end of my trolley: scanner, a squashed protein bar, and tonight's rate sheet saying 112 per cent, which means the target goes up next week. That's how they reward you here. Break ends in four minutes. Love to all non-pickers.

units.title: Night power cuts. Week two.
units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Starting a fresh thread as the old one is now mostly freezer advice. Ours went at 23:40 last night and came back at 02:15, the third night out of four. Questions, in order: 1. Is the school opening if it goes again tonight? 2. Does the Co-op actually pay out for a freezer full of fish fingers? 3. How is everyone with little ones managing the dark? Mine have decided the landing is haunted.

units.author: sb_roadworks
units.text: Temp lights at the Brackwater jct went out with the cut again last night, so it was a free-for-all at 06:00. Two vans and a tractor doing the polite dance. Honestly smoother than when the lights work. Council, please take note: the junction is better with no signals at all.

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: Lineman here. I'll leave the school to the school. On the rest: we're running the Tollinby side with spare crews and it trips at night, not in the day. A full chest freezer kept shut holds eight hours or more, so don't open it to check. The claims form is on the Co-op site under 'domestic losses'. Flaming long form, mind, so put the kettle on first.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Thank you, that's more use than anything on the Co-op page. Eight hours is fine, it's never been off more than three. I'll fill the form in during the next cut, by candlelight, like a Victorian with a grievance.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Readings for anyone matching cuts to weather. Carrow Point last night: 1031 hPa and steady, wind under 2 knots, dew point minus 3, visibility over 20 km. No fog, not a wisp. I've been back through my log, and two of this week's trip nights were exactly the same, clear as a bell. The Met Office will tell you the same if you ask nicely. Make of that what you will.

units.author: sb_lostcat
units.text: Mill Lane, Port Ammet. Ours went at midnight. Pebble sat on the kitchen windowsill the whole time staring at the dark garden and wouldn't come up to bed, which she has never done. For anyone new, she's grey with one white sock and she was missing ten days earlier this month, so I worry about everything now. Thank you to everyone who checked their sheds back then.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Lads, it's the cold. Old cables, cold snap, things trip. Happens every winter. You just never had a forum to moan on before.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Brisk, I've lived here forty years and a cold snap has never taken the lights out four nights in five. But thank you for your input, as always. I've written it on the fridge.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Forty years and now you've got a forum to post it on. Like I said. Buy a torch and go to bed early.

units.author: lineman_tess

edit.note: edited: typo in the fourth trip time
edit.text: Cross-checked against wx's station. Our trips last week, rounded: 23:52, 00:40, 01:15, 23:10, 02:05. The station had fog on the first three nights and none at all on the fourth and fifth. So two clean trips on clear, dry, still nights. Corrosion tracking needs salt and damp together. I'm an apprentice and I might be missing something, but I'd really like someone to tell me what.

units.text: Cross-checked against wx's station. Our trips last week, rounded: 23:52, 00:40, 01:15, 22:10, 02:05. The station had fog on the first three nights and none at all on the fourth and fifth. So two clean trips on clear, dry, still nights. Corrosion tracking needs salt and damp together. I'm an apprentice and I might be missing something, but I'd really like someone to tell me what.

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: Tess is right and she did that on her own time. Clear nights, no fog, breakers going like something's leaning on the line, and when we patrol there's nothing there. I've said it before and I'll keep saying it until somebody tells me to stop.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Tollinby square went dark at 01:50. I was awake anyway, as ever. It is very quiet when every fridge in the street stops at once. I could hear the clock on the memorial, which I hadn't known still ticked. Power back at 02:30, and the lamp the council forgot came on first, as if it had been waiting.

units.title: Daft question. Lamp in the window?
units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Possibly a daft question. My eldest came home saying her friend's family in Gilliver keep a lamp lit in the front window all night 'so they know the house is awake', and with the cuts she wants us to do it too. Is that a real thing or a sleepover story? And if it's real, does a battery lantern count? I am not leaving a candle burning with three kids and a spaniel.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Ha. Next you'll be putting salt on the doorstep. It's a light. Get a nightlight from the cheap shop on the high street and tell her it's magic.

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: Dear, it is a real thing in Gilliver. My mother kept a lamp in the front window every night of her life and so do I. It is only manners, the way you would leave the porch light on for somebody coming home late. A battery one is perfectly all right. Nobody minds what sort of lamp. Kind regards from the Harbour Row end.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: Lisle does it too, though not as much as Gilliver... my gran had one in the kitchen window facing the slip. I always thought it was for the boats. Ha, anyway, I've started doing it again this week. No reason. It's cosy.

units.author: sb_lostcat
units.text: We did this when Pebble was missing, a lamp by the back door so she'd see her way home. She came back on the tenth night. I'm not saying it was the lamp, but I haven't switched it off since, and my electricity bill has opinions about that. Thank you all again.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Aye, what she says. Most of the front windows along the harbour have one. My father lit ours before he lit his pipe, every night, and nobody ever said why and nobody asked. A battery one's fine. My daughter uses a bike lamp on a saucer.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Thank you both, that's lovely and a lot less spooky than my daughter made it sound. Bike lamp on a saucer it is. Brisk, your nightlight suggestion has been noted and the children have overruled it.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: Your funeral. When they want a lamp for the goldfish as well, don't come crying to the Sound Board.

units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: I've kept a lamp in the shop window for years, though I always told myself it was to sell books to other insomniacs. Perhaps I'm Gilliver at heart. Your daughter has good instincts. Every house is better for looking awake, and the fish-finger freezer will forgive you.

units.title: Kittering Holm. Camp lights seen from Gilliver. Continued.
units.author: sb_mod
units.text: Continued from the previous thread, which has reached a length the forum software dislikes. The usual reminders apply. Sources for claims, please. No speculation about named individuals working on the island: they are people doing a job and some of them have family reading this board. Thank you.

units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: Just asking questions. Why does a land-clearing job need lights all night? Why can nobody at the council tell me the end use? Why buy an island with nothing around it, for cash, through a front? 'Somewhere with nothing around it' is the definition of a refuge. The rich have bunkers abroad. Why not here? Do your research.

units.author: propwatch_ledger
units.text: Finding 1: the intermediary that bought the Holm has filed nothing since the purchase. No building warrant, no utilities application, no harbour works licence. Finding 2: if it were a refuge, I'd expect at least a jetty application by now. I could be wrong, I have been before, but the paperwork is very quiet.

units.author: skeptic_planner
units.text: Because a camp has people living in it, and people need light at night. A vegetation clearance does not have to state an end use; the conditions on this one cover reseeding and run-off, not building. Islands with nothing around them are cheap per hectare and nobody objects to plans for them. That's land speculation. It's dull, which is exactly why it's likely.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Out to the creels at five this morning. Holm side lights were four or five points again, one low and orange, a fire likely. I said fewer the other night. Back to normal now, near enough. That's all I've got. I don't go closer than the Skerry buoy after dark, and the buoy's not lit this week either.

units.author: sb_mod
units.text: A gentle note: 'do your research' is not a source. If you have a document, please link it. If not, please mark speculation as speculation so readers can weigh it. I'll leave the post up. Thank you.

units.author: truthwatch_gil
units.text: Fine, consider it speculation. But speculation is how every real story starts. Someone has sent me photos of the camp lights taken from Gilliver with a long lens and I'm waiting for permission to post them. Watch this space.

units.author: ex_grieve_corran

edit.text: Lights all night is normal on a camp. We had a genny going and a work light on the yard. You leave it on.

units.text: Lights all night is normal on a camp. We had a genny going and a work light on the yard and nobody switched it off, not once, not even when the fuel was low. I won't go into why. Just that you leave it on.

units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: I might be wrong, but I can see the Holm from my kitchen window too. Last night the low orange light went out at about half one and the white ones stayed on. I don't know what that means. Probably someone banked the fire and went to bed. Sorry, I usually only read here.

units.title: Night crossings back from tomorrow. Details.
units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: Sound Lines bulletin says night sailings resume tomorrow, first one the 22:40 from Port Ammet, with 'additional deck and slipway lighting'. Six nights of being stuck on Lisle after eight unless I paid for a water taxi. Nobody has said what the welfare review found, or whether it found anything, which I assume means staff shortages. I'll take the boat back either way.

units.author: skeptic_ferrous
units.text: A practical observation. The review was announced after crews reported someone on unlit slipways at night. Brighter slipways deter trespass and make it easier to see who is there and how tall they are. Whatever the review found, more light is the sensible response to the reports as they were actually made.

units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: Can confirm the lighting part, since I spent two days fitting it. Two LED floods on the foredeck, one aft, a bigger searchlight on the wheelhouse roof, all rewired onto the main bus with the genset as backup so a shore cut can't leave us dark. The harbour's put temporary towers on both slips. It's bright. You'll probably see the boat from Weyhaven.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: The tower on our slip went up yesterday... it's so bright the gulls sit under it all night like it's a beach. I'm on shift for the first boat back tomorrow. Ha, anyway, I'm glad. I think. You can see right to the end of the slip now, where the weed starts.

units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: Seth, thank you, that's the first actual information anyone has given us. Visible from Weyhaven sounds about right for Sound Lines: everything is either missing or excessive. Will report back on the 22:40 tomorrow, assuming it leaves at 22:40, which would be a first.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Saw the Gilliver tower from the water coming in. Lit up like the fair. Mind the glare coming alongside, Seth, our lot say it blinds them at the harbour mouth until they're past the wall.

units.title: Slipway. A dare, apparently.
units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: My grandson works the fryer at the chippy on Saturdays. Says one of the lads there has been telling folk he stood at the end of the Gilliver slip one night in the fog week, in his dad's long coat, for a dare. Ten pound. Not the first foggy night, a later one. I'm only passing it on as I heard it. Make of it what you like.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: Well that's... one of them. Ha. I suppose. The Lisle one wasn't a Gilliver lad, though. Nobody's walking nine kilometres of water in a long coat. I don't know. I'd like it to be a kid. Honestly I would.

units.author: skeptic_brisk
units.text: There it is. Three weeks of 'figures' and 'crew welfare reviews' and it's a kid in a coat for a tenner. Told you all from the start. Grow up.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Brisk, that's one lad, one night, by his own account to a chip shop queue. It isn't 'all of them'. Though if it was a dare I'd like a word with whoever paid the tenner, because the ferry crew were properly shaken and one of them left the job.

units.author: morrow_unknown
units.text: Sorry if this is strange, but I live near the slip and I was up most nights that week. I remember one night of laughing on the harbour wall very late and a car door banging, which might fit a dare. I don't think that was the first night. The first night was quiet. I remember because the foghorn was the only sound.

units.title: Floods on the night boat
units.author: ferry_engineer_seth
units.text: For the lads asking about the new kit: we finished the night boat yesterday. Two LED floods forward, one aft, wheelhouse searchlight swapped for the bigger unit, all on the main bus with the genset as backup so a shore cut doesn't leave us dark at the linkspan. Harbour's towers are up at Gilliver and Lisle. Testing alongside tonight. If your windows face the slip, sorry in advance.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: about time. blackout tape and blinds at the chandlery lads, ten percent off if you say Seth sent you, he can explain it to his wife

units.author: harbourmaster_quill
units.text: Thank you, Seth. For the record: two temporary lighting towers have been placed at the Gilliver slip head and one at Lisle, under the harbour authority's powers. Please do not move or adjust them. Byelaw 14 continues to apply to the slip at all hours. Questions about the welfare review should go to Sound Lines, not to the harbour office. Thank you.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Floods are good. I'd have liked them three weeks ago. For what it's worth I'm on the first one back tomorrow. Same boat, same slip, same me.

units.author: lisle_crew_ada
units.text: Lisle tower's on its own generator for now because the pier supply keeps tripping with the cuts. It's loud... you can't hear the water at all. Not sure if that's better or worse, ha.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Came in past the slip tonight. You could read the paper on the end of it. First time in my life I've seen the weed line at the bottom of that slip after dark. Didn't much like it, if I'm honest. Too bright for what it is.

units.title: That dare story
units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: Somebody's going round saying a kid did it for a dare. Fine. Maybe on one night somebody did. The one we hailed was taller than the lower bracket on the slip lamp post, dark coat to the ground, no light, stood right where the water starts. I hailed twice on the loud-hailer. A kid in his dad's coat would have run or waved. It did neither. The height doesn't fit the prank.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: kerris nobody here is calling you a liar. dare chat goes on the sound board though, this board is for working folk and tide times

units.author: harbourmaster_quill
units.text: I've heard the same story. If any young person was on the slip at night, that is a byelaw matter and I will deal with it with the family, quietly, as I would any other. I won't comment beyond that, and I'd ask others not to name anyone either.

units.author: ferry_mate_kerris
units.text: It's work if it happened at work. I'll stop posting about it here when people stop telling me what I saw from my own deck.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Kerris, the lad they're on about is five foot six in his socks. I've known him since he was in a pram on the harbour wall. I'll say no more than that.

units.title: Breakers again
units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: Another call-out last night, Gilliver spur, 00:40. Breaker opened, auto-reclose, opened again, lockout. We drove the line with the big lamp. Nothing on it. No birds, no branches, no ice, insulators clean as a whistle. Office says salt-fog corrosion. There was no fog, and I've been doing this twenty-five years. It's like something's leaning on the line, and then it isn't.

units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: I was on that patrol. The reclose went twice, so whatever it was cleared and then came back. The nearest pole to the trip point is the one by the Holm road layby. I walked the span with the torch. Frost on the conductors, untouched, all the way along both sides.

units.author: harbour_admin
units.text: garvey the chandlery freezers have lost six hours this week. if it's leaning on the line tell it to lean somewhere else. serious question, are we due a planned cut or is it all faults

units.author: lineman_garvey
units.text: All faults as far as I know. No planned work till next month. Run the freezers off the shore genny if you've got one spare. Flaming nuisance, I know, and I'm sorry for it.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Frost on the line and no fog. Aye. My father would have had a word for that but I'll not put it on here. Mind yourselves on that layby, the verge drops.

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Garvey, for your 00:40: my station read 1032 hPa, wind 1 to 2 knots, relative humidity 71 per cent, no fog, visibility 22 km. A textbook calm, cold night. Salt fog wants humidity well over 90. I've put the week's figures in the Sound Board cuts thread as well.

units.author: lineman_tess
units.text: Thank you, wx. That makes two trips on nights your station had as clear. I've posted the full cross-check in the Sound Board thread so it's all in one place and nobody can say I'm hiding it.

units.title: Reservoir edge, night of the 24th: small session
units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: With the calm spell holding I'd like one more go before the rain. Plan: night of the 24th, north shore of the reservoir below the dam path. Two omnis on stands 40 m apart, the parabolic on the tree line, the handheld as backup. Gain set for peaks around -18 dB, 48 kHz. Small group, quiet, no torches pointed at the woods. Post here if you want to come. Make of it what you will.

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: ok so I'm in!! bringing the zoom thing and my two little omnis, and I'll sync the clocks properly this time, I've got a GPS time app now, nobody mention the one-minute thing. ok so. north shore, dam path. what time?

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Set up from 23:00, record 23:30 to 03:30 if it stays dry. Bring layers; it was minus four at the dam last night and the stands frost up. And yes, sync the clocks. I'll do a clap test at the start so we can align everything afterwards.

units.author: lowband_mod
units.text: Pinned for the session. Reminders: raw files only, note your gain and positions, and please stay off the estate side of the fence. The Brackwater ranger has asked nicely twice. Good luck with the cold, and post the clap test.

units.title: Harbour hum: still looking for the pump
units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Update on the harbour clip. Went down again last night at the same state of tide. Hum's there, about 50 Hz with a wobble, loudest near the end of the east pontoon. Every boat on that pontoon was unplugged from shore power, I checked the bollards. So it isn't a fridge on a boat. That's a pump somewhere on the quay. I'll find it.

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Quick analysis of your posted spectrum: fundamental at 49.6 Hz, strong second harmonic, slow beat at roughly 0.3 Hz. That looks like two motors near mains frequency drifting against each other. A pump plus a compressor would do it. I'd check the fish market's chiller plant before anything more interesting.

units.author: hobby_binaural
units.text: Headphones on for this one. It sits low and dead centre for me, no direction at all, which you'd expect with water carrying it. Honestly it sounds like my mum's caravan fridge on a summer night. Totally mundane and a bit cosy.

units.title: Lights on. Still hearing them.
units.author: dc_7_irena
units.text: Dear neighbours, I wish to thank Mr Jem the electrician, as the stairwell lights have stayed on between six and eight all week and I can see every step. I must also say, so that it is written down, that yesterday at about eleven in the morning I heard the footsteps behind me again from eight to six, and they stopped when I stopped, in full daylight. I am not frightened of the dark. I am only telling you. Irena, 7C

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Thanks Irena. I've asked Jem if he'll pop on here and answer a couple of questions, since half the building is asking me and I print leaflets for a living, I don't know relays. Please keep it civil, everyone. Bev, DCRA

units.author: relay_sparky
units.text: Jem here. Relay on the 6-8 riser was knackered, contacts pitted, timer drifting. New one's in and tested, lights on and staying on. Bev asked about the daylight footsteps. Honest answer: while I was up the step ladder on 7, I heard someone come down from 8 and stop on the landing above me. I said 'all right?' and nobody answered. I assumed a resident who didn't fancy a chat. Not my department. Jem

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Jem, did you see them or only hear them? Stairwells are acoustically odd. A fire door closing on 9 can produce a step-like transient that seems to come from one flight up. I'm not dismissing you, only asking exactly what you observed.

units.author: relay_sparky
units.text: Only heard. Didn't look up, I was holding a cable I'd rather not let go of. Could've been a door. Could've been your compressor. I'm a sparky, not a priest. Jem

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: Irena, I believe it. I still take only the lift, since two weeks now, even when it smells of the bins. If you want, knock on 8B in the morning and I walk down with you before my van. I leave 06:15. Sorry for spelling.

units.author: dc_9_tobin
units.text: For the record, Hollis: a door transient is 1 event. I have one file from the new-lights period, recorded by dc_7 on her phone with her permission. n=11 distinct steps, spacing 0.58 s, regular, daylight, lights on. That is not a door. I am not asserting what it is. I am asserting what it is not.

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: irena i believe you, which is not a sentence i'd have typed three weeks ago lol. i went down at lunch today on purpose to check and got nothing, just the bin store smell and the radiator ticking. but i'm not the cardio of doom's judge anymore. i'll walk down with you too if benedikt's van is early

units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: For what it's worth (not much, I'm the one who put a chair against the roof door), I heard someone go up past 14 tonight at about one o'clock. Lights on, door shut, chair exactly where I left it this time. I'm sketching the landing again because my hands want something to do.

units.title: Rope Walk recycling. Week four.
units.author: sb_bins
units.text: For the council's benefit, as I am told they read this board: the blue bins on Rope Walk were due on the usual day and are still on the pavement this morning, now wearing frost. The newsletter said 'normal service has resumed'. It had, for exactly one week. I await the explanation with interest. Bernard (Rope Walk)

units.author: dc_3_wendell
units.text: Bernard, in Weyhaven our block's bins have been out since Friday and the shop has started stacking boxes against them. At least yours are only frosty. I drove the number 14 for thirty years and the bin lorries were late then too, and they parked across the stop.

units.author: parent_tollinby
units.text: Tollinby's were emptied yesterday, Bernard, so the lorry is out there somewhere. Possibly lost. Possibly frozen to a verge on the Brackwater road. Check under the frost.
